stories.headline: At least 68 killed as high-speed trains collide near Toledo, Spain's second deadly rail crash this year
stories.summary: A high-speed train ran into another that had stopped on the tracks near Urda, in Spain's Toledo province south of Madrid, on Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens, according to the Castilla-La Mancha regional government. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke from the site and promised to find out urgently what happened. It is Spain's second deadly rail collision this year, after a January crash in Andalusia killed 46.
stories.why_it_matters: Spain's high-speed trains carry millions of commuters and tourists a year, and a second deadly crash in ten months will put pressure on the government and the rail operators to explain what failed and what they will change.
stories.background: Spain has built Europe's largest high-speed rail network over three decades, and since 2021 private operators have competed with the state rail company, Renfe, on its main routes. In January, a train run by the private operator Iryo derailed near Adamuz in Córdoba province and was struck by a Renfe train; the Financial Times puts that toll at 46. Wednesday's crash happened in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha. Pedro Sánchez leads a Socialist-led government, and Óscar Puente is its transport minister.

facts.text: A high-speed train ran into another train that had stopped on the tracks near Urda in Toledo province on Wednesday.

stories.headline: Israel's election leaves neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with a majority
stories.summary: Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won the 61 seats needed for a majority in Tuesday's Israeli election, partial results show. With more than 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's bloc had 53 seats, Eisenkot's 48 and Arab parties 19, according to The Times of Israel. Axios said the result points to weeks of coalition bargaining.
stories.why_it_matters: Israel's next government will set its course on the war with Iran, Gaza and Lebanon, which affects regional security and energy prices; Israeli bonds and the shekel fell on the result.
stories.background: Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset, is elected by nationwide proportional representation, so governments are coalitions that need at least 61 seats. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, has led a right-wing and religious coalition since the 2022 election, through the Gaza war that followed Hamas's October 2023 attack and this year's war with Iran. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, heads the main opposition bloc, and his party led Likud in pre-election polls. Arab-led parties have rarely been part of Israeli governments, which is why their seat count matters for any coalition.

facts.text: Votes were still being counted on Wednesday after Tuesday's election, with no clear winner.
With more than 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's bloc had 53 seats, the Eisenkot-led bloc 48 and Arab parties 19, The Times of Israel reported.
A government needs 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats, and both blocs were projected to fall short.
Netanyahu's outgoing coalition lost its majority, and his bloc lost a significant number of seats compared with the 2022 election.
Turnout was the highest in nearly three decades, the BBC reported.
Arab parties made marked gains, and The Hindu reported they hold the key to any majority.
To form a government, Eisenkot would need either the Arab parties or members of Netanyahu's alliance, The New York Times reported.
Israel's president urged against holding a new election despite the inconclusive result.
Israeli bonds and the shekel fell after the vote.
A Times of Israel poll before the vote showed Eisenkot with a big lead over Netanyahu but both blocs short of a majority.

stories.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami on a US visa after leaving Brazil
stories.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing senator who lost Brazil's presidential runoff to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday, landed in Miami with his wife and two daughters after leaving Brazil through Argentina. The State Department extended visas to the family, The Hill reported, citing AP. Brazilian police had canceled his passport in connection with a Supreme Court investigation into alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion.
stories.why_it_matters: The main target of a Brazilian criminal investigation is now in the US with US-issued visas, adding to strains between the Trump administration and the government of Brazil, Latin America's largest economy.
stories.background: Lula, a leftist, won a fourth term on Sunday against Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of President Trump. Flávio is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering, and after his loss a Supreme Court ruling barred him from leaving Brazil and ordered him to surrender his passports. He refused to concede for two days and threatened to try to annul the result before he left. Relations between Washington and Brasília were already tense: in August the Trump administration revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador to the US in a dispute with Lula's government.

He arrived on a private jet, the BBC reported.

stories.headline: Iran rejects ideas in new Qatari peace draft as US reportedly warns Gulf of renewed strikes
stories.summary: Qatari mediators gave Iran a new draft deal on Sunday to end its war with the United States and Israel, an official briefed on the talks said, but an Iranian official said Wednesday that the latest mediation held only unacceptable ideas, Reuters reported. Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that the US has warned several Gulf Arab states it may launch a short, intense round of strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
stories.why_it_matters: The war has pushed up fuel prices well beyond the Middle East, so whether it ends in a deal or flares up again after the midterms affects what people pay for gasoline, heating and travel. The Pentagon puts the US military's cost so far at more than $47 billion.
stories.background: The United States and Israel have been at war with Iran this year, and US and Israeli strikes have damaged Iranian nuclear sites this year and last. President Trump has said stopping Iran's nuclear program was one of the main reasons for the war. Qatar, a Gulf state that hosts a large US air base and also keeps channels open to Tehran, has been mediating. The fighting has raised fuel costs worldwide, and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have been firing missiles at Saudi Arabia.

facts.text: Qatari mediators presented Iran with a new draft deal on Sunday to end the war, and Tehran was expected to respond by the end of the week, an official briefed on the talks said.
An Iranian official said the latest mediation contained only unacceptable ideas, Reuters reported.
The US has warned several Gulf Arab states that it may carry out a short but intense renewal of the war after the Nov. 3 midterms, The Wall Street Journal reported; other outlets followed its report.
The Journal reported signs that US and Israeli forces are preparing a possible wave of strikes to push Tehran into negotiating.
President Trump said the war will end 'when I want it to,' CNBC reported.

The war had cost the US military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to military estimates reported by Reuters, CBS News and The New York Times; Reuters said that is more than 25% above the Pentagon's July estimate.
Bombs, missiles and other munitions made up more than 60% of that cost, The New York Times reported.
Rafael Grossi, head of the UN nuclear agency, said there was no sign that Iran has tried to repair nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli strikes.

stories.headline: Cyclone Arnab hits India's east coast, killing at least three
stories.summary: Cyclone Arnab came ashore in Andhra Pradesh in eastern India early Wednesday with winds of about 125 km/h, killing at least three people and damaging homes and crops, according to AP and Reuters; The Hindu later reported five deaths in the state. Authorities had moved tens of thousands of people out of coastal areas, and the storm is heading north toward Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and West Bengal.
stories.why_it_matters: Heavy rain is forecast across four more Indian states as the storm moves inland, putting homes, farms and power lines at risk, and AP noted that the coast it hit is lined with data centers worth billions of dollars. Coverage in the digest came only from left-leaning and center outlets.
stories.background: Cyclones form over the Bay of Bengal in most years, and the October-to-December season often brings them ashore in India's eastern states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, which have large low-lying coastal populations. The India Meteorological Department issued red alerts for both states ahead of landfall, and evacuations began the day before. AP reported that Arnab strengthened over unusually warm ocean water and tied it to a wider rise in extreme weather.

facts.text: Cyclone Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast early Wednesday, officials said.
The storm struck with winds of about 125 km/h (78 mph), France 24 reported.
At least three people were killed, and homes, farmland and crops were damaged.
The Hindu reported five deaths in Andhra Pradesh and said families of the dead would receive ₹5 lakh (500,000 rupees) each.
Heavy inflows were swelling rivers across three districts of northern Andhra Pradesh.
The storm is heading for Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and West Bengal, where heavy rain is forecast.

stories.headline: Knife attacker, a minor, shot dead after wounding officer at Israel's embassy in Belgrade
stories.summary: An attacker armed with knives wounded a police officer guarding the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade just after midnight Wednesday and was shot dead by the officer, Serbian authorities said. Officials said the attacker was an underage male who had been monitored by security services, and The New York Times reported that the government said he appeared to support the Islamic State group and called the attack terrorism.
stories.why_it_matters: Israeli diplomatic sites in Europe are under armed police guard, and this attack, by a minor already known to Serbia's security services, comes as the country's government changes hands after an election that ended Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years in power.
stories.background: Israel's embassy in Belgrade is guarded by officers from the Gendarmerie, an elite unit of Serbia's police. Interior Minister Ivica Dacic, who gave details of the attack, belongs to the outgoing government: a student-led movement won the Oct. 25 election, and Vucic, Serbia's dominant leader for 14 years, conceded defeat. The Islamic State group, which once held territory in Iraq and Syria, has inspired attacks by individual supporters across Europe, some of them teenagers.

facts.text: An attacker with knives went after a police officer from an elite unit guarding the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade just after midnight Wednesday, and the officer shot him dead, police said.

The government said the attacker appeared to be an Islamic State supporter, and authorities described the attack as terrorism, The New York Times reported.

stories.headline: Houthis say they hit Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery; oil prices rise
stories.summary: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement said Tuesday it struck Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom's biggest, with a ballistic missile. Blasts were heard in Riyadh, where Saudi Arabia said its air defenses intercepted Houthi missiles. Oil prices rose more than 1% on Wednesday on renewed supply worries.
stories.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia is the world's second-largest crude producer, so attacks on its oil sites can lift crude prices and, in turn, what drivers and households pay for fuel.
stories.background: The Houthis, an armed movement backed by Iran, control much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, and fought a Saudi-led military coalition for years after 2015. They have also attacked shipping in the Red Sea. During this year's war involving Iran, they have spent weeks firing at Saudi oil and civilian targets, including Riyadh's international airport, according to The Hindu. Ras Tanura, on the Gulf coast of Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, is a major hub for the state oil company, Saudi Aramco.

facts.text: The Houthis said they hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile on Tuesday.
Ras Tanura is Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery, Reuters reported.
Blasts shook Riyadh, and Saudi Arabia said its air defenses intercepted Houthi missiles over the capital.
Oil prices rose more than 1% on Wednesday after the attack.
Saudi Arabia has faced weeks of Houthi strikes on oil and civilian sites, including Riyadh's international airport, The Hindu reported.
Houthi missiles also struck an airport in Yemen, and a spokesman said they were targeting a Saudi cargo plane, The Washington Times reported.

stories.headline: Egyptian court orders independent news site Mada Masr closed and fines its editor
stories.summary: A Cairo court convicted Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, of running an unlicensed website on Tuesday and ordered one of Egypt's last independent news outlets to close. Attalah was taken into custody pending payment of a fine and has since been released, The Guardian reported. Amnesty International and the Committee to Protect Journalists condemned the ruling.
stories.why_it_matters: Mada Masr is one of Egypt's last independent news outlets, so closing it leaves Egyptians with fewer sources of news outside state-aligned media. Coverage in the digest came only from left-leaning and center outlets.
stories.background: Egypt under President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi, in power since 2013, has kept tight control of the media, and press-freedom groups have long ranked it among the countries that jail the most journalists. Mada Masr, which Attalah co-founded in 2013, publishes investigative reporting from inside Egypt and has faced repeated legal pressure, including a block on its website. Egyptian law requires news websites to hold a license from a state media regulator, the basis for this conviction.

facts.text: The New Cairo Misdemeanours Court convicted Lina Attalah of operating an unlicensed website and ordered Mada Masr shut down.
Attalah was taken into police custody pending payment of the maximum fine, according to Amnesty International.

Amnesty International called the ruling a devastating blow to media freedom.
The Committee to Protect Journalists condemned the conviction and urged Egyptian authorities to reverse it and release Attalah.
Reuters described the case as one seen as a test for independent media in Egypt.
